chapter.name: Kinetic Theory
chapter.blurb: The chapter explains the behaviour of gases from the idea that a gas is a collection of rapidly moving molecules. It derives the pressure of an ideal gas, interprets temperature as the average kinetic energy of a molecule, and recovers the gas laws. It then uses the law of equipartition of energy to predict the specific heats of gases and solids, and introduces the mean free path.

concepts.name: Molecular nature of matter
concepts.description: The atomic (molecular) theory of matter, the laws it explains, the sizes and spacings of atoms in solids, liquids and gases, the nature of the interatomic force, and rough estimates of molecular volume, molecular size and intermolecular distance.
concepts.idea: Matter is made of atoms and molecules in perpetual motion; in a gas they are so far apart that the short-range forces between them hardly matter, which is why gases are the simplest state to understand.
concepts.rule: Dalton proposed the atomic theory to explain the laws of definite and multiple proportions. Gay Lussac's law: when gases combine chemically to yield another gas, their volumes are in the ratios of small integers. Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases at equal temperature and pressure have the same number of molecules. The size of an atom is about an angstrom (10^-10 m). In solids and in liquids atoms are a few angstroms (about 2 angstrom) apart; in gases the interatomic distances are tens of angstroms and the mean free path is thousands of angstroms. The interatomic force has a long range attraction and a short range repulsion and is important only when atoms are close. A gas is in dynamic equilibrium: molecules collide and change speed and only average properties stay constant. Estimates: mass of a molecule = molar mass / Avogadro number; if the molecules of a liquid are closely packed, volume of a molecule = mass of a molecule / density of the liquid; when the volume available per molecule grows by a factor f, the spacing grows by f^(1/3).
concepts.example: Water: 1 mol has mass 0.018 kg, so one molecule has mass 0.018/(6 x 10^23) = 3 x 10^-26 kg and volume (3 x 10^-26 kg)/(1000 kg/m^3) = 3 x 10^-29 m^3.

concepts.name: Behaviour of gases: the ideal gas equation and the gas laws
concepts.description: The ideal gas equation in its several forms, the Boltzmann constant, Avogadro number, the mole and molar volume, the meaning of an ideal gas, and Boyle's law, Charles' law and Dalton's law of partial pressures as consequences.
concepts.idea: At low pressures and high temperatures every gas obeys one simple relation between pressure, volume, temperature and amount, and the familiar gas laws are just that relation with something held fixed.
concepts.rule: PV = mu R T, where mu is the number of moles, T is the absolute temperature in kelvin and R = N_A k_B = 8.31 J/mol K. Since mu = M/M0 = N/N_A (M mass of gas, M0 molar mass, N number of molecules), PV = k_B N T and P = k_B n T, with n the number of molecules per unit volume and k_B = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K. Also P = rho R T / M0 with rho the mass density. The Avogadro number is 6.02 x 10^23 per mol; 1 mol of any ideal gas at STP (273 K, 1 atm) occupies 22.4 litres. A gas that satisfies PV = mu R T exactly at all pressures and temperatures is an ideal gas; real gases approach it at low pressures and high temperatures, where the molecules are far apart and their interactions negligible. Fixed mu and T: PV = constant (Boyle's law). Fixed mu and P: V proportional to T (Charles' law). Mixture of non-interacting ideal gases: P = P1 + P2 + ..., where P1 = mu1 R T / V is the partial pressure of gas 1 (Dalton's law of partial pressures).
concepts.example: 1 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K in a vessel of volume 0.02493 m^3: P = mu R T / V = 1 x 8.31 x 300 / 0.02493 = 1.0 x 10^5 Pa.

questions.q: Starting from PV = mu R T, obtain the relation between the pressure P of an ideal gas, its mass density rho, its molar mass M0 and its absolute temperature T. Then use your relation to find the density of nitrogen (M0 = 0.028 kg/mol) at a pressure of 8.31 x 10^4 Pa and a temperature of 280 K. Take R = 8.31 J/mol K.

questions.a: Sample answer: start with P = 2 atm, V = 3 litres, T = 300 K. Stage 1 (constant temperature, Boyle's law PV = constant): the pressure is reduced to 1 atm, so V = 2 x 3 / 1 = 6 litres at 300 K. s: Stage 1 at constant temperature with numbers satisfying PV = constant
Stage 2 at constant pressure with numbers satisfying V proportional to absolute temperature (temperatures in kelvin)
Shows PV/T is the same at the start and at the end

concepts.name: Pressure of an ideal gas from kinetic theory
concepts.description: The assumptions of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas and the derivation of the pressure from the momentum that molecules give to a wall in elastic collisions.
concepts.idea: The pressure of a gas is the momentum that its randomly moving molecules deliver to each unit area of the wall each second.
concepts.rule: Assumptions: a gas is a very large number of molecules in incessant random motion; the interaction between molecules is negligible except during collisions, so they move freely in straight lines between collisions; all collisions between molecules and with the walls are elastic, so total kinetic energy (and, as usual, total momentum) is conserved. A molecule of mass m hitting a wall parallel to the yz-plane has its x-component of velocity reversed, v_x to -v_x, while v_y and v_z are unchanged; its momentum changes by -2 m v_x, so momentum 2 m v_x is imparted to the wall. In time dt the molecules with x-component v_x that hit an area A of wall number (1/2) n A v_x dt (half of those in the volume A v_x dt, the other half moving away). Momentum transferred Q = (2 m v_x)((1/2) n A v_x dt), so P = Q/(A dt) = n m v_x^2, and summing over all groups P = n m (mean of v_x^2). The gas is isotropic, so mean of v_x^2 = mean of v_y^2 = mean of v_z^2 = (1/3)(mean of v^2), giving P = (1/3) n m (mean of v^2). The shape of the vessel is immaterial (A and dt drop out), and collisions between molecules do not change the result because the gas is in a steady state.

concepts.name: Kinetic interpretation of temperature and rms speed
concepts.description: The link between the pressure-volume product and the translational kinetic energy of the molecules, the meaning of temperature as average kinetic energy per molecule, and the root mean square speed and how it depends on temperature and molecular mass.
concepts.idea: The absolute temperature of a gas is a measure of the average kinetic energy of one of its molecules, whatever the gas.
concepts.rule: With N molecules, PV = (2/3) E, where E = N x (1/2) m (mean of v^2) is the total translational kinetic energy. Combining with PV = k_B N T gives E = (3/2) k_B N T, so the average translational kinetic energy per molecule is (1/2) m (mean of v^2) = (3/2) k_B T: proportional to the absolute temperature and independent of the pressure, the volume and the nature of the ideal gas. The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. The root mean square (rms) speed is v_rms = sqrt(mean of v^2) = sqrt(3 k_B T / m); at the same temperature lighter molecules have the greater rms speed, and for two gases at one temperature the rms speeds are in the inverse ratio of the square roots of their molecular masses. In a mixture in equilibrium the average kinetic energy per molecule is the same for every gas, which gives P = (n1 + n2 + ...) k_B T, Dalton's law of partial pressures.
concepts.example: Nitrogen at 300 K: m = 28/(6.02 x 10^26) kg = 4.65 x 10^-26 kg, mean of v^2 = 3 k_B T/m = (516)^2 m^2/s^2, so v_rms = 516 m/s.

concepts.name: Law of equipartition of energy and degrees of freedom
concepts.description: Translational, rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom of monatomic and diatomic molecules, the squared terms in the energy of a molecule, and the law that each such term carries an average energy of (1/2) k_B T.
concepts.idea: In thermal equilibrium the energy of a gas is shared equally among all the independent ways (modes) in which a molecule can hold energy.
concepts.rule: A molecule has one degree of freedom for motion along a line, two for motion in a plane and three for motion in space; a molecule free to move in space has three translational degrees of freedom, each contributing a squared term such as (1/2) m v_x^2. A monatomic gas (argon) has only these three. A diatomic molecule treated as a rigid rotator (O2 at moderate temperatures) has in addition two rotational degrees of freedom, about two axes normal to the line joining the atoms, each contributing a term such as (1/2) I omega^2; rotation about the line joining the atoms does not count. Some molecules (CO) also have a vibrational mode even at moderate temperatures; one vibrational mode contributes two squared terms, kinetic (1/2) m (dy/dt)^2 and potential (1/2) k y^2. Law of equipartition of energy: in equilibrium at absolute temperature T the total energy is equally distributed among all possible energy modes, each mode (each squared term) having average energy (1/2) k_B T. So each translational and each rotational degree of freedom contributes (1/2) k_B T, and each vibrational mode contributes 2 x (1/2) k_B T = k_B T. Average energy per molecule: monatomic (3/2) k_B T; rigid diatomic (5/2) k_B T; diatomic with one vibrational mode (7/2) k_B T.
concepts.example: Rigid diatomic gas at 320 K: 5 squared terms, so the average energy per molecule is (5/2) k_B T = 2.5 x 1.38 x 10^-23 x 320 = 1.10 x 10^-20 J.

concepts.idea: Counting the energy modes of a molecule tells us how much energy a mole of the substance takes up per kelvin, and that is its molar specific heat.
concepts.rule: Per mole. Monatomic gas: U = (3/2) R T, C_v = dU/dT = (3/2) R, C_p = (5/2) R, gamma = C_p/C_v = 5/3. For any ideal gas C_p - C_v = R. Rigid diatomic gas (5 degrees of freedom): U = (5/2) R T, C_v = (5/2) R, C_p = (7/2) R, gamma = 7/5. Diatomic gas with one vibrational mode: U = (7/2) R T, C_v = (7/2) R, C_p = (9/2) R, gamma = 9/7. Polyatomic gas with 3 translational, 3 rotational degrees of freedom and f vibrational modes: C_v = (3 + f) R, C_p = (4 + f) R, gamma = (4 + f)/(3 + f). With R = 8.31 J/mol K the predictions ignoring vibration are C_v = 12.5, 20.8 and 24.93 J/mol K for monatomic, diatomic and triatomic gases, in good agreement with several gases; for gases such as Cl2 and C2H6 the measured values are larger, and including vibrational modes improves the agreement. Heat needed = number of moles x molar specific heat x rise in temperature, with C_v at fixed volume and C_p at fixed pressure. Solids: each atom vibrates in three dimensions with average energy 3 k_B T, so U = 3 R T per mole and C = 3 R, which agrees with most solids at ordinary temperature (carbon is an exception).
concepts.example: 1 mol of argon (monatomic) heated through 10 K at constant volume needs 1 x (3/2) x 8.31 x 10 = 125 J.

concepts.name: Mean free path
concepts.description: Why molecules of finite size collide, the time between successive collisions, the mean free path and its dependence on number density and molecular diameter, and numerical estimates.
concepts.idea: Because molecules have a finite size they keep colliding, so although they move very fast they travel only a short average distance, the mean free path, between collisions.
concepts.rule: Take the molecules as spheres of diameter d. A molecule moving with average speed <v> collides with any molecule whose centre comes within a distance d of its own; in time dt it sweeps a volume pi d^2 <v> dt and so suffers n pi d^2 <v> dt collisions, n being the number of molecules per unit volume. The average time between successive collisions is tau = 1/(n pi <v> d^2), and the mean free path, the average distance between two successive collisions, is l = <v> tau = 1/(n pi d^2) if the other molecules are imagined at rest. Since all molecules move, the collision rate depends on the average relative velocity and a more exact treatment gives l = 1/(sqrt(2) n pi d^2). The mean free path depends inversely on the number density and on the square of the diameter; in a highly evacuated tube it can be as large as the tube. At a fixed pressure the number density is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature. In a gas at ordinary conditions the mean free path is about 100 times the distance between molecules and about 1000 times the size of a molecule.

Its path is an incessantly deflected zigzag, so although its speed is large its net progress across the room is slow and the gas takes a considerable time to diffuse.
s: Judgement: wrong - the molecule collides after a very short distance (the mean free path) and its direction keeps changing
So it does not move straight across the room; the net spreading (diffusion) takes considerable time despite the large speed
